content.title: About
content.content: Basil (Ocimum basilicum) is a fragrant herb in the mint family, native to tropical regions of Asia. It has a slightly sweet, mildly peppery flavor with notes of anise and clove. Basil is used fresh or dried in pesto, salads, tomato dishes, pasta, and drinks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Basil is related to mint, lemon balm, and rosemary.
There are hundreds of varieties, including sweet (Genovese), Thai, lemon, and purple basil.
Classic pesto is made from basil, olive oil, cheese, pine nuts, and garlic.
Holy basil (tulsi) is a different species, Ocimum tenuiflorum, widely used in India.
Basil loves warmth and is sensitive to cold: its leaves turn dark at low temperatures.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Basil leaves contain vitamin K, which plays a role in blood clotting.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The essential oils and polyphenols in basil have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: The body can partly convert the carotenoids in green leaves into vitamin A.

items.title: Adds flavor without extra salt
items.content: Fresh herbs make dishes aromatic without needing much salt or fat.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: In small amounts, basil provides calcium, iron, and magnesium.

items.title: Vitamin K and blood thinners
items.content: People taking anticoagulants such as warfarin should not suddenly change how much vitamin K-rich greens they eat without consulting a doctor.

items.title: Concentrated oils and extracts
items.content: Basil essential oil and concentrated extracts contain compounds that should not be taken in large amounts, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Basil allergy is possible, especially in people sensitive to other plants in the mint family.

items.title: Pesto is energy-dense
items.content: Ready-made pesto contains a lot of oil, salt, cheese, and nuts, so portions should be moderate, and people with nut allergies should check the ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tear fresh basil leaves by hand and add them at the end of cooking to preserve their aroma. Use basil in salads, pizza, pasta, and dishes with tomato and mozzarella, make it into pesto, or add it to drinks. Dried basil is less fragrant and can be added earlier in cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh basil dislikes cold: do not keep it unprotected on cold refrigerator shelves, or the leaves will blacken. Stand the stems in a glass of water at room temperature, or wrap them in a slightly damp paper towel and store for a few days. Basil can be frozen, for example as pesto or chopped with oil. Keep dried basil in an airtight jar away from light.

content.title: About
content.content: Toasted cinnamon bread consists of slices of bread toasted to a golden crisp and flavored with ground cinnamon. It offers a sweet‑spicy taste and a crunchy texture, making it perfect for breakfast or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cinnamon is one of the oldest spices, used in cooking for over 4,000 years.
Toasting intensifies the cinnamon aroma and gives the bread a satisfying crunch.
In many countries toasted cinnamon bread is served with butter or cream cheese.
The sweet spice combined with slightly bitter toasted bread creates a balanced flavor profile.
Toasted bread is often used in desserts such as French toast.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions supply dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants from cinnamon
items.content: Cinnamon is rich in polyphenols, which may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood sugar regulation
items.content: Some studies suggest cinnamon can improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing aroma
items.content: The scent of cinnamon is often linked to improved mood and reduced stress.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions may contain added sugar, which is unsuitable for diabetics.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Toasted bread with butter and cinnamon can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Excess cinnamon intake
items.content: Large amounts of cinnamon (especially cassia) may lead to excess coumarin, which can be harmful to the liver.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toast slices until golden, sprinkle with ground cinnamon, and optionally drizzle with honey or maple syrup. Serve with butter, cream cheese, or as a base for fruit toppings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bread in a cool, dry place in an airtight bag. Toasted slices are best consumed within 2–3 days, otherwise they may become soggy. For longer storage, freeze the slices and re‑toast before eating.

bread-multigrain-reduced-calorie-and-or-.title: Multigrain Bread, Reduced Calorie, High Fiber, Toasted

content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain toasted bread with reduced calories and high fiber is a whole‑grain loaf made from a blend of several grains, seeds and bran, then toasted to a golden crust. It offers a crunchy texture and rich flavor while providing fewer calories and more dietary fiber than regular white bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Multigrain breads typically contain 5–8 different grains, such as oats, barley, rye and whole wheat.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crisp crust while preserving most nutrients.
The high fiber content helps regulate blood sugar and supports digestive health.
Calorie reduction is achieved by using whole‑grain flours with lower energy density and adding leavening agents that create a lighter crumb.
Many multigrain breads are fortified with B‑vitamins and minerals like iron and magnesium.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety and helps control blood glucose levels.

items.title: Reduced calorie content
items.content: Lower energy density makes the bread suitable for weight‑management diets without sacrificing taste.

items.title: Rich in micronutrients
items.content: The grain blend provides vitamin E, magnesium, zinc and iron, supporting metabolism and immunity.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs release energy slowly, maintaining stable energy throughout the day.

items.title: Heart‑healthy benefits
items.content: Fiber and healthy fats from seeds help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Grain allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to wheat, rye or other grains used in the loaf.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The bread contains gluten and should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Certain varieties may contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread as a snack, in sandwiches, as toast, or alongside soups and salads. A toasted slice pairs well with avocado, low‑fat cottage cheese, turkey, or vegetable spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags and re‑toast before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Buffalo sauce is a spicy condiment made from butter, vinegar, hot sauce (usually cayenne‑based), and seasonings. It is named after Buffalo, New York, where it was first created in the 1960s as a topping for chicken wings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original recipe was developed at the Anchor Bar in 1964.
The combination of butter and hot sauce gives a flavor that is both fiery and creamy.
Buffalo sauce is used not only on wings but also on vegetables, seafood, burgers, and even as a marinade.
There are many heat levels, from mild to extreme (the infamous "Molotov" version).
In the United States, buffalo sauce is considered a classic "game‑day" sauce, often served at football matches.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin in the hot sauce may boost metabolism and provide a mild analgesic effect.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vinegar and spices contribute small amounts of B‑vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Butter provides vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: High capsaicin levels can irritate the stomach and esophagus in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Butter makes the sauce calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Buffalo sauce is traditionally tossed with fried chicken wings, but it can also be added to meat marinades, burger sauces, salad dressings, or used as a dip for vegetable sticks and cheese appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in an airtight jar in the refrigerator. At 4 °C it retains flavor and quality for 2‑3 months. Before serving, let it reach room temperature so the butter does not separate.

chicken-or-turkey-salad-made-with-light-.title: Chicken or Turkey Salad with Light Italian Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey salad with light Italian dressing is a mix of fresh leafy greens, diced boiled poultry, tomatoes, cucumbers and sometimes cheese, tossed with a delicate dressing made from olive oil, vinegar, lemon juice and aromatic Italian herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are lean protein sources that readily absorb the flavors of the dressing.
Light Italian dressing typically contains less sugar and fewer calories than traditional creamy sauces.
Poultry salads are often served in Mediterranean restaurants as a refreshing dish in warm weather.
Adding nuts or seeds boosts healthy fat content and makes the meal more satiating.
The salad can be prepared ahead, but the dressing should be added just before serving to keep the greens crisp.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Lean poultry pieces and a light dressing keep saturated fat levels low, supporting heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The salad supplies vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as potassium and magnesium from the vegetables, aiding immunity and nerve function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Leafy greens and added vegetables deliver fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, peppers and herb‑based dressing are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly cooked or stored poultry can harbor salmonella or campylobacter.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Store‑bought dressings can contain added salt; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Commercial dressings may include preservatives or sweeteners that are not suitable for all consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, tossing the greens, diced chicken or turkey and dressing together just before eating. Optional toppings include nuts, seeds, avocado or a sprinkle of light cheese for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Store the dressing separately to maintain crispness. Ensure cooked poultry is fully cooled before refrigerating.

content.title: About
content.content: A whole egg, fried without added salt, is a staple dish in many cuisines worldwide. The egg provides protein, fat, vitamins, and minerals, while frying gives it a distinctive flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried eggs can be prepared in just a few minutes, making them a quick breakfast option.
The yolk contains almost all of the egg’s nutrients, including vitamin D and choline.
The "sunny side up" method keeps the yolk runny, whereas "over hard" fully cooks it through.
Eggs come in various sizes; in the US a "large" egg is the standard for recipes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: One large egg provides about 6 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2), and biotin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Choline is important for liver function and brain development, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Lutein and zeaxanthin
items.content: These carotenoids promote eye health and may protect against age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: The yolk contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, including a modest amount of omega‑3.

items.title: Salmonella
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella bacteria; it is advisable to cook eggs until the yolk is fully set.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: A yolk contains roughly 186 mg of cholesterol; individuals with elevated cholesterol should moderate intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white proteins are common allergens, especially in children.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Heat a small amount of oil in a skillet, crack the egg in, and cook 2–3 minutes to the desired doneness. For "sunny side up" do not flip; for "over easy" gently flip and cook an additional minute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw eggs in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C in their original carton, up to 3–4 weeks. Cooked fried eggs should be eaten within 2 hours at room temperature or kept refrigerated for up to 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard pretzels are baked wheat flour snacks known for their golden crust and iconic knot shape. They have a slightly salty taste, a crunchy texture, and are commonly enjoyed as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels originated in Europe, and their shape is said to represent crossed arms in prayer.
Hard pretzels are often sprinkled with coarse sea salt or flavored with spices such as paprika and garlic.
In the United States more than 2 billion pretzels are consumed each year.
Mini‑pretzel bites are popular for office snack packs.
There is a World Pretzel Day celebrated on April 26.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Hard pretzels provide quick‑digesting carbs for an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, they contain little fat when baked without added oils.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The wheat flour used supplies a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions add fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: Pretzels can contribute thiamine and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of their simple carbs, pretzels can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The salty coating may be a concern for those monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pretzels contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While low in fat, large portions can add up in calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard pretzels are convenient as a standalone snack, paired with cheese, mustard, hummus, or used to add crunch to salads and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp toast is a popular Asian appetizer consisting of a slice of bread that is fried until golden and topped with a mixture of minced shrimp, egg, herbs, and spices. The toast is served hot, often accompanied by soy sauce or a sweet‑spicy dipping sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Hong Kong in the 1970s and quickly became a beloved street‑food staple.
Traditional filling uses finely chopped shrimp, sometimes combined with crab meat or other seafood.
Some recipes add corn starch to the batter for an extra‑crisp crust.
Shrimp toast is usually served in bite‑size pieces, perfect for eating with the hands.
In Japan a similar snack is called “Ebi Toast” and is often served with a mayo‑based sauce.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide a high‑quality, easily digestible protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat‑based snacks, shrimp contain very little saturated fat and cholesterol.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of selenium, zinc, and iodine, which support immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Shrimp contain astaxanthin, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although low in saturated fat, shrimp do contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Added fats
items.content: Preparation often involves breadcrumbs and oil; excess oil can raise the calorie count of the dish.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Fresh seafood must be cooked thoroughly to prevent foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve shrimp toast hot, cut into bite‑size pieces. Dip it in soy sauce, sweet‑spicy chili sauce, or a flavored mayo. It is commonly garnished with lime wedges and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed within 2–3 hours of cooking. If you need to store, let it cool to room temperature, then place in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef tamale is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a corn masa dough filled with seasoned stewed beef, wrapped in corn husks and steamed. The dough is slightly sweet and dense, while the beef provides a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales have been prepared in Mexico for over 2,000 years and are considered one of the oldest dishes in the Americas.
They are traditionally made in large batches for celebrations, especially Day of the Dead and Christmas.
There are more than 200 regional filling variations, ranging from sweet fruit to spicy chili and meat.
Corn husks (hojuelas) impart a distinctive aroma and keep the tamale shape during cooking.
In some regions the masa is made from fermented corn flour, which can improve digestibility.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The beef filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Corn masa – carbohydrate source
items.content: Corn provides energy and dietary fiber that promotes digestive health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and corn together supply B6, B12, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Beef can contain saturated fats, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Traditional recipes often use salt and sauces, raising the sodium content.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn products.

items.title: Risk of foodborne bacteria
items.content: If tamales are not cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F), there is a risk of salmonella or other intestinal infections.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are usually served hot, unwrapped from the husk. They can be eaten on their own or topped with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. Fresh cilantro, lime juice, and diced onion add brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag – they keep quality for about 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tequila is a Mexican distilled spirit made from the fermented juice of blue agave (Agave tequilana). Production is strictly regulated and the name is protected by a geographical indication, meaning tequila can only be produced in designated regions of Mexico.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: True tequila can only be made from blue agave; other agave species are used for mezcal.
There are five official categories: Blanco (Silver), Joven (Gold), Reposado, Añejo and Extra Añejo.
Agave plants must mature for at least 8 years before they are harvested for tequila production.
Traditional agave cooking uses a copper "tahona" where the piña is roasted to caramelize sugars.
While often served with salt and lime, in Mexico tequila is frequently sipped neat.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Blue agave is rich in polyphenols, which may help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Moderate consumption supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest moderate tequila intake can raise HDL (good) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Provides inulin
items.content: Inulin is a prebiotic fiber that promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Like any high‑proof spirit, tequila can cause alcohol poisoning when consumed in excess.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of sedatives and anti‑inflammatory medications.

items.title: Agave allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to agave components.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Tequila can be enjoyed neat, chilled, or as a base for cocktails such as Margarita or Paloma. Aged varieties (Reposado, Añejo) are best sipped in a glass that allows aromas to develop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, tequila retains its quality for several years, though the aroma may gradually diminish.
